comment: Data spine for Hardwood Autochess tactics. Counter multipliers are the OFFENSE's efficiency multiplier vs that coverage. Base band is 0.85-1.15 (rock-paper-scissors with teeth, no hard counters); personnel modifiers layer on top, final clamp 0.80-1.25 in tactics.js. Coverage terms mirror Brooks's NBASwiftTactics PuzzleModel.swift vocabulary (Drop, ICE, Switch All, Blitz/Trap).

offenses.name: Spread Pick-and-Roll
offenses.translation: One ball screen up top, four shooters holding the arc — give the defense two bad choices on every possession.
offenses.wants: A downhill handler (speed) plus a floor full of credible shooters.

personnel.note: {name} bends the screen — the spread PnR is only as scary as its downhill handler ({value} speed).
Spacing is credibility: your floor shoots {value} on average, so help defenders have to stay home.

drop.note: Their drop big sagged into the paint and your handler rose up — pull-up jumpers all night. Drop's known bill: it concedes the pull-up to protect the rim.

ice.note: Their ICE pushed every screen down the sideline — no middle, no corner outlet. The spread's math dies on the baseline.

switch.note: They switched to kill the action, but every switch writes a mismatch somewhere — hunt their weakest defender.

blitz.note: Two on the ball, 4-on-3 behind it — a wash: the trap hurt your handler, but four spacers made them pay for gambling.

zone23.note: A zone guards the floor, not shooters — five spacers bend a 2-3 until the corners come open.

offenses.citation: The Hoops Geek: offenses counter low drop by screening higher so the handler can rise into a pull-up 3 (thehoopsgeek.com/basketball-plays/pick-roll-against-low-drop-defense).

offenses.name: Spain Pick-and-Roll
offenses.translation: A normal ball screen with an ambush: a shooter back-screens the dropping big, then pops to the arc.
offenses.wants: A genuine shooting threat to pop, plus enough team speed to run the choreography.

personnel.note: {name} is the popper ({value} shooting) — Spain only works if the back-screener is a shot the defense fears.
Spain is three players moving on a timer — your team speed ({value} avg) sells the choreography.

drop.note: Spain is drop coverage's nightmare: the back-screen ambushed their dropping big, and the popper walked into an open three.

ice.note: Their ICE flattened the screen angle before the back-screen could land — the ambush needs a big who drops, and he never did.

switch.note: Switching keeps a body on every screener — your Spain back-screen hit nothing but a pre-switched defender.

blitz.note: The trap came, but Spain's second screener became the 4-on-3 release valve behind it.

zone23.note: Zone defenders guard space, not screens — Spain's choreography screened the air.

offenses.citation: Hooper University: Spain PnR adds a back-screen on the roll man's defender, demanding coordination from three defenders at once (hooperuniversity.com/breakdowns/ball-screen-offense-spain-pnr-explained).

offenses.name: Zoom (Chicago) Action
offenses.translation: A pindown screen that flows straight into a dribble hand-off — the shooter catches the ball already moving downhill.
offenses.wants: Shooters, plural. Zoom manufactures catch-and-shoot and pull-up looks; it is worthless without them.

personnel.note: Zoom manufactures shooting looks — your floor averages {value}, so the looks it creates actually go in.

drop.note: The pindown-into-handoff put your catcher downhill with their big still dropping — a free runway into a pull-up.

ice.note: ICE is a ball-screen rule; Zoom's hand-off isn't a ball screen. Their coverage never triggered.

switch.note: They switched the hand-off at the exchange — Zoom's whole product is a head start, and the switch erased it.

blitz.note: They trapped the hand-off at the exchange point — your catcher never got downhill with the ball.

zone23.note: Zoom's motion probed the zone's seams; the kick-out three was there whenever the help pinched.

offenses.citation: The Hoops Geek: Zoom (also called Chicago) combines a down screen with a dribble hand-off, creating double and triple gaps for drives and kick-out 3s (thehoopsgeek.com/basketball-zoom-action).

offenses.name: Delay 5-Out
offenses.translation: Your big runs the offense from the top of the key while all five players start beyond the arc — every drive and cut has a runway.
offenses.wants: A playmaking hub big (defense + touch) and cutters with speed.

personnel.note: {name} is your Delay hub — a big who can catch at the top and make a read is the whole engine.
personnel.missingNote: No hub: Delay 5-Out needs a big with hands and touch at the top of the key, and you don't have one.

personnel.note: 5-out is a cutting offense — your team speed ({value} avg) is what turns empty lanes into layups.

drop.note: Five-out cutting into a set rim protector — their drop big just stood where all your cuts finish.

ice.note: ICE wants sideline ball screens; Delay lives at the top of the key, outside ICE's jurisdiction.

switch.note: Even matchups everywhere — your hub kept probing, but their switches kept the floor honest.

blitz.note: They trapped your hub and he short-rolled into a 4-on-3 — five-out spacing makes blitzes bleed.

zone23.note: A 2-3 packs exactly the lanes Delay's cutters need — the rim was walled off before the cut began.

offenses.citation: Basketball Action Dictionary / HoopTalkTV glossaries: in 5-out all five players start beyond the arc, opening the lane for drives and cuts; Delay initiates through the big at the top.

offenses.name: Seven Seconds or Less
offenses.translation: Push off every rebound and every make — get a shot up before the defense can even call a coverage.
offenses.wants: Speed everywhere. Pace is the whole offense.

personnel.note: Pace is personnel: your floor averages {value} speed, and transition efficiency is bought with legs.

drop.note: Drop teams keep their floor balance — their big was already back protecting the rim before your break started.

ice.note: You can't ICE a fast break — but they matched speed with speed. Even money.

switch.note: Transition cross-matches broke their switching rules before they could even set them.

blitz.note: Every failed trap became a runout the other way — pace punishes gamblers.

zone23.note: A zone has to be set to exist — you beat the paint-packers down the floor and it was layup city.

offenses.citation: Cleaning the Glass tracks halfcourt vs transition splits precisely because transition possessions are the most efficient in basketball (cleaningtheglass.com/stats — context estimation of halfcourt vs transition play). Name honors the engine's existing '7 Seconds or Less' synergy.

coverages.name: Drop
coverages.translation: Your big sinks toward the rim on every ball screen: wall off layups and lobs, live with pull-up jumpers.
coverages.wants: A true rim anchor (high defense) stationed in the paint — the back line of your grid.

personnel.note: {name} anchored the paint ({value} defense) — drop coverage is a wall only if the wall is real.
personnel.missingNote: Drop with no rim protector in the paint is a welcome mat — the whole scheme funnels drivers at a big who isn't there.

coverages.citation: Brew Hoop's Bucks dictionary + Slappin' Glass: drop shields a slower big, protects the rim, and avoids rotations — the accepted bill is pull-up jumpers and pick-and-pop 3s (brewhoop.com 'Drop' PnR defense; slappinglass.com drop-and-pop). Wording matches PuzzleModel.swift: 'dropping the big man into the paint... take away the lob threat.'

coverages.name: ICE (Push / Blue)
coverages.translation: On side ball screens, force the handler down the sideline — the baseline becomes your sixth defender.
coverages.wants: On-ball pursuit: your two fastest defenders do the forcing.

personnel.note: ICE is an on-ball chase — the top guards average {value} speed, quick enough to jump the screen and force baseline.

coverages.citation: Basketball Action Dictionary: ICE/Down forces the handler away from the screen toward the sideline (medium.com/thebasketballactiondictionary PnR coverages). Matches PuzzleModel.swift: 'using the baseline as an extra defender.'

coverages.name: Switch Everything
coverages.translation: Trade assignments on every screen: nobody ever gets open, but somebody ends up guarding the wrong guy.
coverages.wants: Five interchangeable defenders — the scheme is only as strong as its weakest switcher.

personnel.note: The defenders are interchangeable (defense spread of {value}) — switching works when every switch is a fair trade.
Every switch eventually lands on {name} ({value} defense) — offenses hunt the weakest link in a switching scheme.

coverages.citation: The Hoops Geek '7 ways to defend the PnR' + Basketball Action Dictionary: switching kills the offense's rhythm and avoids rotations, at the cost of mismatches the offense will hunt. Matches PuzzleModel.swift: 'switching keeps a body on the 3-point shooter.'

coverages.name: Blitz (Trap)
coverages.translation: Send two defenders at the star the moment the screen hits: rip the ball out of his hands and gamble 4-on-3 behind you.
coverages.wants: Energy defenders to trap and recover — and an opponent whose offense runs through one star.

personnel.note: Their offense runs through {name} ({value}% of their board's production) — the blitz takes the ball out of exactly those hands.
Trapping is a sprint economy — the trapping defenders average {value} speed, enough to trap and still recover behind it.

coverages.citation: Hoop Mentality: the blitz traps the handler the moment he uses the screen, forcing the ball out of the star's hands at the cost of a 4-on-3 behind the trap (hoopmentality.com blitz-the-pick-and-roll). Matches PuzzleModel.swift's Blitz/Trap card.

coverages.name: 2-3 Zone
coverages.translation: Guard the floor, not the man: pack the paint, wall off the rim, and dare them to beat you from outside.
coverages.wants: Collective length — team-wide defense keeps the zone's seams closed.

personnel.note: A zone is five closeouts sharing one brain — the team defense averages {value}, so the seams stay shut.

coverages.citation: Coaching consensus (Coach's Clipboard, Basketball Action Dictionary): a 2-3 protects the rim and hides individual defenders, conceding perimeter shots and vulnerable before it is set — hence transition and spacing beat it.
